Like my title says, I'm a game developer whose first attempt at a game failed miserably! We were ambitious and had a great team of dedicated programmers and artists (albeit a small one). Alas the project could not stand the test of time, but we did get major traction moving our project into an almost playable state. It was a great first try, and now, with a skeleton crew of two, I'm trying again. My partner and I have spent just about a month of coding and designing to start a new project, a small, randomly-generated sidescroller that we hath dubbed, Rainsford after the protagonist of the Most Dangerous Game.

Here's a shitty gif: http://www.gfycat.com/CanineTerrificGullGfycat

We're not anywhere close to being finished, but we're almost done with the first level and it feels great. Feel free to ask anything about our past projects, current endeavors, future plans, and African Dwarf Frogs.

And if you'd like any images or gifs I'll do my best to provide them.

Edit: Sorry for the double post, I forgot tags.
[IAMA] failed indie-dev trying to start over! Ask me anything!
How are you planning to advertise your future projects?

Well, assuming that we DO indeed finish our projects and get onto new projects, we'll continue posting on indie-dev and indie-gamer forums (which worked pretty well for our last unfinished game). We've also given consideration to contacting youtube channels that specialize in indie games, and perhaps game media (small journals, steam community etc.). Certain youtube channels especially review your game for you if you give them a copy (mutually beneficial) so we'll definitely be pushing forward on that end

I'm really just spitballing here, but have you considered creating a channel, yourself, that vlogs the process and allows a community to come along for the ride? A lot of the allure to indie games is that these are games made by real people, not giant organizations that are out for their money cough EA cough.

It's a creative approach that I've seen work effectively for mediums that are just as difficult, if not harder, to break into. There are writers and movie/television producers that have taken this approach and ended up selling their scripts and obtaining the studio investments needed to bring their baby into fruition. Providing educational content by sharing their experience built them a large fan-base. I don't see a reason why taking this approach with game development would yield any less.
Thanks, hadn't actually considered that. I guess it wouldn't take much effort on our part to make a quick video every now and then showcasing art and code. I'll look into this more
You're not a failed indie dev. You're an indie dev with a unfinished project who is working on a new project. Don't beat yourself up.
That means a lot /1to34, it certainly isn't easy work but I'm glad people like you can be so supportive of us.

Oh, a minimalistic side scroller! Sounds right up my alley! So, for those of us who aren't familiar with "The Most Dangerous Game," what is it and how do you incorporate it into your game (if at all)?

Thanks for the interest! Well it's a short story about a man who's hunted in an island jungle, by a sadistic rich hunter named Zaroff and his minions. Thus, in our game "Rainsford" you navigate your way through jungle levels and mansion levels, all the while pursued by hounds, Ivan the manservant, and Zaroff himself.
Tell us the gist of your new game? :)

Well going along the lines of The Most Dangerous Game, you're stranded on an island trying to get to Zaroff's mansion before he kills you. Levels are randomly generated in order, not content (that being said I've made QUITE a few levels so there'll be a lot of variety between games). In that way it's a maze game (keeping track of which zones bring you closer) and a side-scrolling survival game. The basis of gameplay is the "door" mechanic, essentially you go through one portal, be it a bush, a door, etc. and come out nearby, bypassing traps, leading enemies into traps, and navigating in a series of AI based puzzles. Given that's it's a rogue-esque game, there'll be items and powerups you can get as well that'll make a new try easier.
How do you support yourselves while doing development work?

Well the good thing about being an "indie" dev (as opposed to being a professional or career dev) is that we don't have deadlines. While this also means we are vulnerable to procrastination, it also means that we have time on the side for part time jobs and whatnot. Personally I work as a paid intern for a tech startup, which is nice. I'm also in college with a decent amount of scholarship money, so lodging and food are both things that I generally don't have to worry about. The same can be said for my friend :)

Depending on where you are, there are chapters of the igda that help bring indie devs together to help them understand the life cycle of development all the way through finishing, promoting and selling your game.

Not only that, but it's always great to be able to physically hang out and spit ball with like minded people.
Wow. Did not even know there was an organization like this. This is fantastic, thanks!
You got it, there may be more than that depending on where you reside. Good luck!

Hi, I'm interested in becoming an indie developer and was wondering if you have any tips or tricks you'd be willing to share... What was the first coding language you learned? What do you recommend for a beginner?

Tips and tricks... Well the first thing you should do is start coding. I personally would suggest Java as it's (in my opinion) easier to learn than C++, and there are a lot more formal courses out there in schools, college, and online that'll help you learn it! Of course you can't go wrong with C++ either. If you are an ABSOLUTE beginner however, I'd suggest you go on code academy and experiment with Python to learn programming fundamentals. The great part about the whole thing is that there are so many libraries out there, it doesn't matter which language you choose. I code in both C++ and Java (though I'm better at java), and I use both SFML and LibGDX libraries (though for this project my partner and I are using C++, and he's doing more coding while I'm doing more art :P). The art itself is, to be honest, actually harder to master. Coding simply takes thought and resources to learn, along with quite a bit of practice. Unless you have some background in color theory and art techniques, you'd probably have more fun doing trial and error with different media, pixel art, vector art etc. and eventually, you will get better.
Thanks man, I'm on the right path then. I'm about a quarter of the way through python on code Academy

What part of the development are you doing? Are you writing code? Are you designing visuals? Maybe both since its such a small team.

Also what platform are you aiming for?

What development environment and language are you using? I'm a programming noob and genuinely curious as I have some assembly, C, C++, C#, and python experience from college but none of it was focused on gaming.

I personally am in charge of art (I use gimp, it's good for pixel art) and level design, as well some coding (AI, entities). My partner is the main programmer, and he does the bulk of the engine designing. So yeah we both do both if you know what I mean :)

We are using SFML, a graphics library, and it should be good for Mac/Windows/Linux and forseeably Ios, coding using Visual Studio 2012. SFML is a C++ language. The languages you know are what traditionally are most used in game development! There are tons of libraries for C++ and python, and I know that certain engines like Unity go great with C#. All you need is knowledge of Object Oriented concepts really, the rest is just legwork from there. Of course it's also helpful to have some Data Structures knowledge, and quite frankly the hardest part is getting to know your library!

Cool. I really appreciate the reply. I've used GIMP tons. I also love InkScape. (Open source shoutout!)

I wish you the best of luck. I have an idea for a game, so maybe I need to flesh it out and try my hand at it. Maybe I can make it in blender or something as a rough concept.
Drawing concept art never hurts! Good look!
I have heaps of ideas for games - do you want them? they are good. i don't care who has them.

Believe me keep them for yourself. I'll never be able to put together exactly what you have in your head, and vice versa. Save them for when you get a team of your own, or maybe take up programming one day and make a game yourself!

you're doing a great job on the art. i wanted to put in a little bit of feedback though, if you're putting in AIs and want to keep that run speed the same i would suggest you either make the foreground objects slightly less visible or smaller. also for the asking, what else are you going to implement in the game to really put your mark on it past the artwork?

Thanks for the feeback on the art, the foreground is definitely something I need to work on so things obscure the main character less. In terms of making the the game unique I'll be experimenting with the gameplay. The minute-to-minute gameplay within each section of the game will be either fast-paced maneuvering around enemies and traps using the door mechanic (short range "portals" that'll take you forward or backward a certain distance) or slow, drawn out spates of crouching and hiding from certain slower, or faster enemies (Ivan the manservant, certain hounds). The order in which you traverse the sections will be randomized, and death will be instantaneous (the dungeon-esque part certainly isn't very unique). We chose to make it randomized because it fit the nature of the game, and the minimalistic art style will allow me in particular to make a huge variety of levels without breaking my fingers. I'm also hoping to add music that gets louder the closer you are to Zaroff's mansion, so you know whether or not you're travelling in the right direction or not, but that part is tentative (according the my programming partner). And of course, if we choose the keep the dungeon-esque part of the game, there'll be outfits and items you can pick up to improve gameplay. Also shown in the gif we have is a "light" mechanic (it's really just a crappy black square with a hole) meant to represent light from a lamp (not shown on his sprite). I have all the sprites and different circles/cones of vision, but I have not added them to the game yet. Hopefully that'll make things a bit more interesting.
